narrative:
The model predicted a 56.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically denied your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA was the single strongest influence, and it worked in your favor. At 3.70 it sits well above the average of accepted students (3.23), pulling the prediction noticeably toward passing. Unfortunately the other two decisive factors pushed harder in the opposite direction.

Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the next most important signals. You placed in the bottom decile in both years (1st and 2nd decile respectively), far below the average 6th-decile performance of students who were admitted. These low rankings outweighed the benefit of your strong GPA and increased the predicted risk of bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score of 28 also sat well below the 37-point average of accepted applicants and added further weight toward a negative outcome, though it was less influential than your class rankings.

Taken together, the model saw a student with solid college grades but consistently weak class standing and a low LSAT, producing a failure probability high enough to justify denial.

What you should do next is straightforward: retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, then consider reapplying once you have improved that key credential.
